questions.question: Mean intensity of solar radiation at Earth is 1.37 kW m^-2 and the Earth-Sun distance is 1.50 x 10^11 m. Show that the Sun's luminosity is about 4 x 10^26 W.

steps: Power spreads over a sphere centred on the Sun with radius equal to the Earth-Sun distance d.
Area of sphere: A = 4 pi d^2 = 4 pi (1.50 x 10^11 m)^2 = 2.83 x 10^23 m^2.
Intensity I is power per unit area, so total power L = I x A.

Mass-energy equivalence: E = delta m c^2.
delta m = 1.4 x 10^17 kg.

questions.question: Explain how a massive planet orbiting a star can cause a change in the wavelength of light received from the star.
questions.answer: The star moves in a small orbit about the star-planet centre of mass, so its line-of-sight velocity changes and spectral lines show a periodic Doppler shift.
steps: The planet and star both orbit their common centre of mass, so the star moves in a small orbit.
When the star moves towards Earth its light is blueshifted; when it moves away it is redshifted.
So the wavelengths of its spectral lines change periodically (Doppler effect).
The size of the shift depends on the star's velocity along the line of sight, which reveals the planet.

questions.question: A spectral line of wavelength 4.35 x 10^-7 m has a maximum shift of 3.19 x 10^-13 m. Calculate the maximum velocity of Gliese 876 away from the Earth.

v = c x delta lambda / lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 x (3.19 x 10^-13 / 4.35 x 10^-7).

questions.question: Explain how the appearance of the HR diagram for a star cluster changes as the cluster gets older.
questions.answer: The main sequence turn-off moves down and to the right as the most massive stars leave the main sequence first and become red giants; old clusters show red giants and white dwarfs.
steps: In a young cluster all stars, including very luminous hot stars, are still on the main sequence.
The most massive stars use their hydrogen fuel fastest, so they have the shortest main sequence lifetime.
When hydrogen in the core runs out they leave the main sequence and expand into red giants (higher luminosity, lower temperature).
So the hot, luminous end of the main sequence is lost: the turn-off point moves down and to the right.
Older clusters therefore show red giants and, eventually, white dwarfs; only lower-mass main sequence stars remain.

questions.question: It is claimed that dust around a standard candle makes it appear farther away than it really is. Assess the validity of this claim.
questions.answer: Valid: dust dims the light, so the measured intensity is too low and the inverse-square method then gives too large a distance.
steps: The distance from a standard candle uses I = L / (4 pi d^2), with L known.
Dust absorbs or scatters light, so the observed intensity I is lower than without dust.
Solving for distance: d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)), so a smaller I gives a larger d.
The claim is therefore valid, unless the dimming is corrected for (for example by using colour data).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by redshift.
questions.answer: An increase in the observed wavelength of light from a source that is moving away from the observer.
steps: Light from a receding galaxy is observed at a longer wavelength than it was emitted.
Spectral lines are shifted towards the red (longer wavelength, lower frequency) end of the spectrum.
This is the Doppler effect: motion away from the observer stretches the wavelength.
Redshift z = (observed wavelength - emitted wavelength) / emitted wavelength.

questions.question: Light from NGC 6052 has redshift z = 0.0158. With H0 = 1.62 x 10^-18 s^-1, calculate the distance of NGC 6052 from Earth.
steps: For small redshift the recession speed is v = z c.
Hubble's law: v = H0 d, so d = v / H0.

questions.question: Two colliding galaxies accelerate towards each other. Explain why the acceleration increases as time passes.
questions.answer: The galaxies get closer, so the gravitational force between them increases (inverse square law) and so does the acceleration.
steps: The galaxies attract each other gravitationally.
As time passes the separation between them decreases.
Gravitational force F = G M1 M2 / r^2 increases as r decreases.
A larger force gives a larger acceleration (F = ma).

questions.question: Describe how trigonometric parallax can be used to determine the distance to a nearby star.
questions.answer: Measure the star's apparent shift against distant background stars at two points six months apart; distance d = 1 AU / parallax angle.
steps: Observe a nearby star against distant background stars at one time of year.
Observe it again six months later, when Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit.
The star appears to shift; half the angle between the two directions is the parallax angle p.
For small angles d = (radius of Earth's orbit) / p, i.e. d = 1 AU / p.

questions.question: Explain how knowledge of the distances to distant galaxies has enabled astronomers to determine a value for the age of the universe.
questions.answer: Distances (standard candles) and recession velocities (redshift) give H0 from v = H0 d; the age of the universe is approximately 1/H0.
steps: Distances to distant galaxies are found using standard candles and the inverse square law.
Recession velocities are found from the redshift of spectral lines.
Hubble's law v = H0 d gives the Hubble constant H0 from the gradient of v against d.
If galaxies have moved apart at a constant rate, their age since the Big Bang is T = d / v = 1 / H0.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a standard candle? A: a star of known distance, B: a star of known intensity, C: a star of known luminosity, D: a star of known mass.
questions.answer: C: a star of known luminosity
steps: A standard candle is an object whose luminosity (total power output) is known.
Its distance is found by comparing this luminosity with its observed intensity: I = L / (4 pi d^2).
Known distance (A) or known intensity (B) alone does not make a standard candle.
Mass (D) is not related to its brightness, so C is correct.

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.

steps: A standard candle is an astronomical object of known luminosity.

questions.question: State what is meant by a main sequence star.
questions.answer: A star fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, in stable equilibrium between gravity and radiation pressure.
steps: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Outward radiation pressure balances the inward gravitational force (hydrostatic equilibrium).
On the HR diagram they lie along a diagonal band from hot, luminous to cool, dim stars.
The Sun is a main sequence star.

questions.question: As a red giant the Sun's radius is about 150 times its current radius and its luminosity about 1600 times. Show that lambda_max is about 1 x 10^-6 m.
questions.answer: lambda_max = 9.7 x 10^-7 m, about 1 x 10^-6 m (surface temperature about 2980 K)
steps: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4, so L / L0 = (R / R0)^2 (T / T0)^4.
Wien's law: lambda_max = b / T = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K / 2980 K = 9.7 x 10^-7 m, about 1 x 10^-6 m.

questions.question: Comment on the value of lambda_max from part (ii) and the classification of the Sun as a red giant. Red light lies between 6.2 x 10^-7 m and 7.8 x 10^-7 m.
questions.answer: lambda_max = 9.7 x 10^-7 m lies beyond the red end of the visible spectrum (infrared), consistent with a cool red giant surface, so the classification is consistent.
steps: Red light spans 6.2 x 10^-7 m to 7.8 x 10^-7 m, so 9.7 x 10^-7 m is longer than red light (infrared).
Most of the peak emission is therefore infrared rather than visible.
A long peak wavelength means a low surface temperature (about 3000 K), typical of a red giant.
A cool star looks red, so the red giant classification is consistent with the value.

questions.question: Explain how the orbital period of a planet changes as the mass of the Sun decreases, assuming the orbital radius does not change.
questions.answer: The period increases: T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)), so T increases as M decreases.
steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: G M m / r^2 = m (4 pi^2 / T^2) r.
This gives T^2 = 4 pi^2 r^3 / (G M), so T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)).
For fixed r, T is proportional to 1 / sqrt(M).
As M decreases, T increases: the planet takes longer to orbit.

questions.question: Humans cannot survive a gravitational field 4 times the Earth's surface value. Kapteyn-b has radius 1.02 x 10^7 m and density 6.44 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Deduce whether humans could survive its surface gravity.
questions.answer: g = 18 N kg^-1, about 1.9 times Earth's surface value, which is less than 4 x 9.81 = 39 N kg^-1, so humans could survive.
steps: Surface gravity g = G M / R^2 with M = (4/3) pi R^3 rho, so g = (4/3) pi G rho R.

questions.question: Describe how stellar parallax is used by astronomers.
questions.answer: Measure a nearby star's position against distant background stars six months apart; the parallax angle p gives distance d = 1 AU / p.
steps: Observe a nearby star against distant background stars at one time.
Observe it again six months later, when Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit.
The apparent shift gives the parallax angle p (half the angle between the two positions).
Use d = (1 AU) / p for small angles to calculate the distance.

The lack of detection was a limit of measurement.

steps: Redshift: z = delta lambda / lambda = (394.5 - 393.4) / 393.4 = 2.80 x 10^-3.

questions.question: Betelgeuse has luminosity 4.49 x 10^31 W and peak intensity at 850 nm. A website claims its radius is 1000 times the Sun's (T_sun = 5800 K, L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W). Assess the accuracy of this claim.

steps: Surface temperature from Wien's law: T = 2.90 x 10^-3 / 8.50 x 10^-7 m = 3410 K.

questions.question: Explain how main sequence stars evolve into red giants and then white dwarfs, referring to the fusion processes occurring in the star.
questions.answer: Hydrogen fuses to helium on the main sequence; the core then burns helium in the red giant phase; the remnant carbon-oxygen core cools as a white dwarf once fusion stops.
steps: On the main sequence, hydrogen fuses to helium in the core, releasing energy that balances gravity.
When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and heats, and hydrogen fuses in a shell around it.
The outer layers expand and cool, forming a red giant with greater luminosity.
When the core is hot enough, helium fuses into carbon and oxygen.
When core helium is exhausted, the outer layers are ejected and the hot carbon-oxygen core remains.
This core is a white dwarf: it no longer fuses and gradually cools.

steps: Protons are positively charged and repel each other electrostatically.

questions.question: The initial estimate of H0 was 1.5 x 10^-17 s^-1, giving an age T. The current estimate is 2.1 x 10^-18 s^-1. What is the age using this value? A: 0.14 T, B: 0.71 T, C: 1.4 T, D: 7.1 T.
steps: The age of the universe is T = 1 / H0, so T is inversely proportional to H0.
The new age is 7.1 T.
Answer D.

questions.question: Astronomers use trigonometric parallax to determine distances to stars. Which must they know? A: distance between the Sun and a nearby star, B: diameter of the Sun, C: distance between the Sun and the Earth, D: diameter of the Earth.
questions.answer: C: the distance between the Sun and the Earth
steps: Parallax distance d = (baseline) / parallax angle.
The baseline is the Earth-Sun distance (radius of Earth's orbit).
The diameter of the Sun or Earth is not needed.
Answer C.

questions.question: Explain why trigonometric parallax can only be used to determine the distance to objects that are relatively close to the Earth.
questions.answer: Parallax angles for distant objects become too small to measure accurately.
steps: The parallax angle p is the baseline divided by the distance, so p decreases as distance increases.
For distant objects p becomes very small.
Such small angles cannot be measured accurately with current instruments.
So only relatively nearby objects can be measured.

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.
questions.answer: An object whose luminosity is known.
steps: A standard candle is an astronomical object of known luminosity.
Its apparent intensity can be measured on Earth.
The distance then follows from the inverse square law.
Cepheid variables are examples.

questions.question: Describe how the method of standard candles is used to determine the distance to a distant star cluster.
questions.answer: Identify a standard candle in the cluster, find its luminosity, measure its intensity, and use I = L / (4 pi d^2) to find the distance.
steps: Identify a standard candle (for example a Cepheid) in the star cluster.
Determine its luminosity from a known property such as its period.
Measure its apparent intensity I at Earth.
Use d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: The radiation emitted by Tau Ceti has maximum intensity at frequency 5.50 x 10^14 Hz. Show that its surface temperature is about 5300 K.
steps: Peak wavelength lambda_max = c / f = 3.00 x 10^8 / 5.50 x 10^14 = 5.45 x 10^-7 m.
Wien's law: T = b / lambda_max = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K / 5.45 x 10^-7 m.

questions.question: Calculate the average kinetic energy of gas atoms at the surface of Tau Ceti.
questions.answer: Average kinetic energy = 1.1 x 10^-19 J
steps: Mean translational kinetic energy of a gas atom: E_k = (3/2) k T.
This uses the surface temperature found in part (a)(i).

questions.question: Planet Aita is 8.05 x 10^10 m from Tau Ceti (radius 5.52 x 10^8 m). A scientist suggests Aita receives the same intensity from Tau Ceti as Earth receives from the Sun (1360 W m^-2). Evaluate this suggestion.
questions.answer: Aita receives about 2.1 x 10^3 W m^-2, about 1.5 times the Earth's value, so the suggestion is not accurate.
steps: Intensity from the star: I = sigma T^4 (R / d)^2.
Earth receives 1360 W m^-2, so Aita receives about 1.5 times as much: the suggestion is not accurate.

questions.question: Complete the nuclear equation for the alpha decay of plutonium-238.
steps: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, 4 2 He.
Mass number: 238 = 234 + 4.
Atomic number: 94 = 92 + 2.

questions.question: Show that the energy released in the decay of one plutonium-238 nucleus is about 5.7 MeV, given m_Pu = 3.9516 x 10^-25 kg, m_U = 3.8851 x 10^-25 kg and m_alpha = 6.6399 x 10^-27 kg.
questions.answer: delta m = 1.0 x 10^-29 kg, so E = 9.1 x 10^-13 J = 5.7 MeV
steps: Mass defect: delta m = m_Pu - (m_U + m_alpha).

questions.question: At launch the decay produced 550 W. A website states there was 1.00 kg of plutonium-238. Given 6.00 x 10^23 atoms in 0.238 kg, half-life 87.7 years and 1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s, deduce whether the statement is accurate.
questions.answer: 1.00 kg gives about 580 W, about 5% above 550 W; 550 W implies about 0.95 kg, so the statement is only approximately accurate.
steps: Half-life T = 87.7 x 3.15 x 10^7 s = 2.76 x 10^9 s; decay constant lambda = ln 2 / T = 2.51 x 10^-10 s^-1.
Activity A = lambda N = 2.51 x 10^-10 x 2.52 x 10^24 = 6.32 x 10^14 decays per second.
Power P = A E = 6.32 x 10^14 x 9.1 x 10^-13 J = 5.8 x 10^2 W, about 5% above 550 W.
So 1.00 kg is only just consistent; 550 W corresponds to about 0.95 kg.

questions.question: The space probe took 74 months to reach Jupiter. Calculate the power produced on arrival due to the decay of plutonium-238 (launch power 550 W, 1 month = 2.63 x 10^6 s).
questions.answer: Power produced = 5.2 x 10^2 W (about 524 W)
steps: Power falls with half-life: P = P0 (1/2)^(t / T_half).

questions.question: Suggest why solar cells were not suitable for a space probe travelling to Jupiter.
questions.answer: Sunlight intensity falls as 1/d^2, so at Jupiter solar cells would receive far too little power.
steps: Intensity of sunlight falls with the inverse square of the distance from the Sun.
Jupiter is much further from the Sun than Mars.
So the solar intensity at Jupiter is much lower, giving much less power from solar cells.
A radioisotope source does not depend on sunlight, so it remains suitable.

questions.question: Hydrogen emits a line at 410 nm on Earth. The same line from a galaxy receding at 0.1c is observed. Which is its wavelength? A: 451 nm, B: 430 nm, C: 410 nm, D: 369 nm.
questions.answer: A: 451 nm
steps: Redshift for v = 0.1c: lambda_obs = lambda_0 (1 + v / c) = 410 nm x 1.1 = 451 nm.
A relativistic check gives 410 nm x sqrt(1.1 / 0.9) = 453 nm, still closest to 451 nm.
A redshift increases the wavelength, so B, C and D are not possible.
Answer A.

questions.question: Describe the stages in the evolution of the Sun from a main sequence star to a white dwarf star.
questions.answer: Hydrogen fusion on the main sequence; core contraction and shell fusion; red giant expansion with helium fusion; ejection of outer layers; a cooling white dwarf remains.
steps: The Sun is on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen to helium in its core.
When core hydrogen is used up, the core contracts and heats, and hydrogen fuses in a shell.
The outer envelope expands and cools: the Sun becomes a red giant with greater luminosity.
When the core is hot enough, helium fuses into carbon and oxygen.
After core helium is used up, the outer layers are ejected, forming a planetary nebula.
The exposed hot core is a white dwarf: no fusion occurs and it gradually cools.

questions.question: Explain why the Sun will stay on the main sequence for a much greater time than the most massive main sequence stars.
questions.answer: Massive stars have much higher luminosity and burn hydrogen much faster, so they use their fuel in a much shorter time.
steps: Time on the main sequence depends on the fuel available and the rate at which it is used.
Massive stars have much higher luminosity because of higher core temperature and pressure.
So they burn their hydrogen much faster.
The Sun is less massive and less luminous, so it uses its fuel more slowly and stays on the main sequence longer.
